$comment: What this repository contributes to a running stack, and what a check may
believe about it. `checked` is proved against this repository by
crates/trailryx-node/tests/manifest.rs in this repository's own CI;
`declared` is a statement nobody can verify and carries its own `why`.
AND THE TWO ROUTINE NAMES ARE COMPONENTS TOO, WHICH THIS FILE FIRST GOT WRONG.
estate.json's `runs` carries ROUTINE names and the first version of this file
carried only BINARY names, so C15 correctly reported that the registry names
two things this repository declares nothing about. idryx and verdryx had
already set the pattern -- `idryx-detect` and `verdryx-drift` are components
there, each mapping to a binary and a subcommand -- and this file broke it.
`trailryx-seal` and `record-seal` are both `trailryx-node events`; the two
names exist because the three launchers schedule it differently.
TEN BINARIES, AND estate.json NAMES NONE OF THEM. Its `runs` list is
`trailryx-seal` and `record-seal`, which are ROUTINE names in two launchers,
both of which run `trailryx-node events`. That is not a mistake in either
file: a registry records what a deployment installs, and this records what
the repository builds. They answer different questions and only the second
one can see a binary nobody installs.
AND THAT IS WHY `dev-tool` EXISTS AS A CLASS HERE.
tokenfuse-cluster, one repository over, is built, tested, CI-gated and
installable by nothing, and has been for fifty-seven days. Seven of the ten
binaries here are ALSO installed by nothing, and that is correct: they are a
demo, a JSONL reader, a kill test, a rate measurement, a reproducer, a
coverage printer and a federation probe. Without a way to say so, a check
that looked for uninstalled components would flag seven right answers here
and be switched off before it ever reached the one real finding next door.
So `dev-tool` means: nothing should install this, and its absence from every
deployment is not a finding. `service` and `tool` mean the opposite, and for
those the absence IS worth asking about.
THE PUBLISHED IMAGE CARRIES ONE OF THE THREE. ghcr.io/taipanbox/trailryx
ships `trailryx-ingest`, and every sealing command lives in `trailryx-node`,
which is published nowhere. stack-k8s records this in its own
images/trailryx.Dockerfile and builds the sealing image from source because
of it.
TRAILRYX_TRUST_DOMAIN IS NOT LISTED AND THAT IS DELIBERATE. stack-k8s sets it
in a ConfigMap and interpolates it into `--trust-domain` in a shell argument.
No code in this repository reads it, so it is the deployment's variable and
not this repository's, and declaring it would put a name here that nothing
in this tree would ever answer for.

nothing_should_install_it.why: One federation peer, or one query across several, from a command line.
Prints what a pack proves next to what each claim needs.

what_it_is.why: The OTLP receiver, and the ONE binary the published GHCR image carries.

nothing_should_install_it.why: Reads a file or a pipe, for looking at one journal by hand.
The kill run: a real process, a real disk, a real SIGKILL.

what_it_is.why: The sealing tool. Every deployment's record profile runs `trailryx-node events` and then `read --pack`.

nothing_should_install_it.why: The append-rate measurement, against a real filesystem.
One command to reproduce any run.

what_it_is.why: The offline verifier a pack is checked with, and the only binary here with no dependency on the rest.

it_is_a_routine_name_not_a_binary.why: The name stack-up's routines.sh and stack-k8s's CronJob use for `trailryx-node events` over the shared bus. estate.json's `runs` carries routine names, so this is the component that name refers to.
The same work under stack-single's name for it: a long-running compose service rather than a scheduled job, because compose has no cron. Two names for one command, which is why both are here.
